did_you_know.text: The chapter opens after Joshua’s death: the Israelites turned to the LORD and asked which tribe should be the first to go up and fight the Canaanites.
Judah invited Simeon to cooperate: each tribe pledged to help the other in its territory.
Adoni-bezek said that seventy kings whose thumbs and big toes had been cut off used to gather scraps under his table, and he saw his fate as retribution for his deeds.

The men of Judah captured Jerusalem, struck its inhabitants with the sword, and set the city on fire; later in the chapter, it says that the Benjamites did not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem.
Caleb offered his daughter Achsah to the man who conquered Kiriath-sepher, that is, Debir; Othniel son of Kenaz captured the city.
Achsah asked Caleb for springs of water as well, and he gave her the upper and lower springs.
The chapter says that Judah drove out the inhabitants of the hill country, but could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had iron chariots.
The Benjamites did not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, and the text says that the Jebusites lived there with the Benjamites until the time when the chapter was written.
In Bethel, a man who showed the house of Joseph the entrance to the city was spared along with his family; afterward, he built a city in the land of the Hittites and named it Luz, its former name.
Several tribes did not drive out the inhabitants of the Canaanite cities but instead subjected them to forced labor. Thus the Canaanites remained in the land even after Israel had grown stronger.
